title: Algorithmic thinking, inputs, processes and outputs
footer: 2.1 Lesson 3: Algorithmic thinking, inputs, processes and outputs
starter: Write the steps you take to get from waking up to leaving the house. Swap with a partner: could they follow yours exactly?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: What an algorithm is
facts: An algorithm is a sequence of steps that solves a problem.
It must be unambiguous: every step means exactly one thing.
It must finish: a set of steps that never ends is not an algorithm.
stations.challenge: Write your own definition of an algorithm, then say why a recipe qualifies.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: An algorithm is a sequence of steps that solves a problem.
Also credit: It must be unambiguous: every step means exactly one thing.

questions.q: Which of these is a requirement of an algorithm?
questions.a: Every step is unambiguous and the whole thing finishes

questions.q: Why is 'stir until it looks right' not a good algorithm step?
questions.a: It is ambiguous: different people would do different things

stations.name: Algorithmic thinking
facts: Algorithmic thinking means working out the steps, and the order they must happen in.
It includes spotting when steps repeat, and when a decision changes what happens next.
A solution found this way works for every similar problem, not just one case.
stations.challenge: Write the steps to find the largest number in a list, without naming a language.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Algorithmic thinking means working out the steps, and the order they must happen in.
Also credit: It includes spotting when steps repeat, and when a decision changes what happens next.

questions.q: Put these steps for finding the largest number in a list into a sensible order.
questions.a: Set the largest so far to the first item → Look at the next item → If it is bigger than the largest so far, make it the new largest → Repeat until the end of the list → Output the largest

questions.q: Why is an algorithm more useful than solving one case by hand?
questions.a: It works for every similar problem, not just the one in front of you

stations.name: Inputs, processes and outputs
facts: Input: the data the problem needs to start.
Process: what is done with that data.
Output: what comes back out at the end.
stations.challenge: Give the inputs, processes and outputs for a program that works out a pizza bill.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Input: the data the problem needs to start.
Also credit: Process: what is done with that data.

questions.q: For a cash machine, is each one an input, a process or an output?
questions.a: The PIN typed by the customer = Input; The amount requested = Input; Checking the PIN is correct = Process; Reducing the account balance = Process; The cash dispensed = Output; The receipt printed = Output

questions.q: A program asks for two numbers, adds them and shows the total. What is the process?

stations.name: Working a problem
facts: Start by asking what the answer needs to be, then what data is needed to get it.
Write the steps in the order they must happen, then check for missing cases.
Test the steps on paper with a small example before writing any code.
stations.challenge: Work out the inputs, processes and outputs for a program that decides if a year is a leap year.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Start by asking what the answer needs to be, then what data is needed to get it.
Also credit: Write the steps in the order they must happen, then check for missing cases.

questions.q: Put these stages of solving a problem into order.
questions.a: Decide what the output should be → Work out what input is needed → Write the steps that turn the input into the output → Test the steps with an example by hand
It tells you what the program must produce, which decides what input and steps you need

stations.name: A worked example
facts: A game of pick-up sticks: 27 sticks, two players, each takes one, two or three.
The one who takes the last stick loses.
Decompose it, then write the steps: set up, take turns, check for the end, declare the loser.
stations.challenge: Write the steps for a two-player pick-up sticks game.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A game of pick-up sticks: 27 sticks, two players, each takes one, two or three.
Also credit: The one who takes the last stick loses.

questions.q: Put the steps of a pick-up sticks game into order.
questions.a: Set the pile to 27 sticks → Ask the current player how many to take, between one and three → Take that many from the pile → If sticks remain, swap to the other player and repeat → When the pile is empty, the player who took the last stick loses

questions.q: Where does the algorithm need a decision rather than a step?
questions.a: Checking whether any sticks are left, which decides whether to carry on

stations.name: Answering algorithm questions
facts: Write steps, not prose: one instruction per line.
Use the same names throughout, and say where a step repeats.
If the question gives a scenario, use its words: sticks, players, pile.
stations.challenge: Plan a six-mark answer describing the steps of a vending machine.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Write steps, not prose: one instruction per line.
Also credit: Use the same names throughout, and say where a step repeats.

questions.q: Which is the better algorithm step?
questions.a: IF the amount entered is more than the balance THEN show an error

questions.q: A student writes an algorithm with no way of stopping. What is wrong?
questions.a: An algorithm must always finish, so it isn't an algorithm yet

final.name: Final challenge: in, through, out

questions.q: For a library self-service kiosk, is each one an input, a process or an output?
questions.a: The barcode scanned from the book = Input; The borrower's card number = Input; The date the book is due back = Output; Checking whether the borrower owes a fine = Process; Working out the due date from today = Process; The receipt printed for the borrower = Output; Marking the book as on loan in the database = Process; The message shown on the screen = Output

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: State what is meant by an algorithm.
points: An algorithm is a sequence of steps that solves a problem.
It must finish: a set of steps that never ends is not an algorithm.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: A program asks for a temperature in Celsius and outputs it in Fahrenheit. Identify the input, the process and the output.
points: An algorithm is a sequence of steps that solves a problem.

It must finish: a set of steps that never ends is not an algorithm.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: In a game, two players take turns removing one, two or three counters from a pile of twenty. The player who takes the last counter loses. Write an algorithm for this game.

The one who takes the last stick loses.
Decompose it, then write the steps: set up, take turns, check for the end, declare the loser.
An algorithm is a sequence of steps that solves a problem.
It must finish: a set of steps that never ends is not an algorithm.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
